items.basis: Phononic crystal structures reduce thermal conductance through phonon scattering, but stiction is primarily an electrostatic adhesion phenomenon, not thermal; the proposed mechanism addresses the wrong physical cause of failure.

The claimed 50% reduction in stiction failures after 10000g shock testing violates the boundary condition of frequency response below 10kHz, as phononic crystal structures would inherently alter the mechanical resonant frequencies of the comb fingers.

The provided evidence [doi:10.1109/iic.2015.7150884] explicitly states that structural modifications to comb fingers must maintain mechanical integrity to preserve sensitivity, directly contradicting the claim that phononic crystal structures won't alter electrical capacitance between fingers.

The prediction of 50% reduction in stiction failures equals the baseline because the candidate provides no evidence that phononic crystals outperform existing anti-stiction coatings (such as self-assembled monolayers) already used in MEMS accelerometers.

Fabricating two-dimensional phononic crystal structures on MEMS comb fingers with the required precision is impossible with current CMOS MEMS foundry processes, as cited in [doi:10.3390/mi17060732], which documents standard fabrication limitations.

The testable prediction fails to specify the exact phononic crystal pattern geometry that would achieve the claimed 50% reduction, making it impossible to validate since the novel design variable (pattern geometry) is not quantified.
